McDonald’s chases customers who are trying to slim down
McDonald’s wants to remodel its restaurants and become a place where people go when they’re trying to eat less but still want protein.

McDonald’s is rolling out a turnaround plan called NEXT. Detailed at an investor day on Sept. 23, the plan includes upgraded chicken and protein menus and costly restaurant remodels that franchisees will pay for largely on their own. Those franchisees own about 95% of McDonald’s restaurants, and their profits are already being squeezed as traffic falls.

McDonald’s already has more than 40% of the $50 billion beef category in its 10 largest markets. The chicken market is larger and growing faster. McDonald’s wants to increase its share by 1.5 percentage points by 2030, which would be worth roughly $2 billion a year.

That’s why the NEXT plan includes higher-quality, hand-breaded chicken. McDonald’s is also adding grilled chicken and exploring chicken bowls and egg bites for people on GLP-1 drugs, who tend to want smaller portions and more protein.

One of the challenges to have better chicken is their kitchen. McDonald’s said in October that a pilot project in Dublin will test whether restaurants can serve hand-breaded chicken consistently with minimal complexity and disruption in the kitchen.

“I think that’s going to be a challenge because it’s more labor-intensive,” said Ari Felhandler, an equity analyst at Morningstar who tried the chicken at the company’s investor day. “I must say the chicken did taste a lot better.”
The upgrades, including a regular remodel as well as kitchen update, would cost McDonald’s franchisees about $1.2 million per restaurant, said Jim Sanderson, an analyst at NorthCoast Research.

“Franchisees are not making as much money,” said Jonathan Maze, editor in chief of Restaurant Business, who has covered McDonald’s for about 20 years. “McDonald’s has to convince franchisees to do this.”

McDonald’s has promised about $8.5 billion through 2036 in rent relief and money toward the upgrades. The company says the changes will add about $100,000 a year in cash flow at an average U.S. restaurant and pay for themselves in about four years.

“Even with partner relief from MCD corporate in the form of rent reductions over time, the cash cost for the total remodel package is too high for many operators to drive a reasonable return on the investment,” Sanderson said.
McDonald’s is also looking to leverage its menu transformation to attract a new wave of GLP-1 users.

“Menu options are for the most part based on products already sold in stores, so changes will not have a significant impact on operations or workflow,” Sanderson said. “I believe this is a smart way to capture market share as consumer demand from GLP-1 users evolves.”
Diana Yi is a 27-year-old freelance photographer in Houston. Yi is a loyal McDonald’s customer who often orders through Uber Eats when there’s a discount.
“McDonald’s is not my first choice when I want healthier food,” said Yi. “I’d probably just cook for myself.”
McDonald’s says 84% of GLP-1 customer households patronize its restaurants, and in April, the company added protein labels to 17 menu items on its app and self-service ordering kiosks.
Yi never noticed the new protein labels.

“High protein was already a trend. GLP-1 is just driving it,” said Michelle He, who holds a Ph.D. in biomedical engineering from the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill and is a bodybuilding enthusiast. “Changes that look appealing in the macro numbers may not entirely add up to a healthier meal.”

McDonald’s also wants to win customers back on price. In late April, McDonald’s launched 10 items under $3 but dropped app deals and a popular “Buy One, Add One for $1” offer. U.S. comparable sales rose only 0.8% in the second quarter, and Chief Executive Chris Kempczinski later said the company had “made a bad trade.”
“People were really mad at that change, and they felt that was a worse deal,” Maze said. “Many people did the math.”

Quick-service restaurants like McDonald’s “are more reliant on lower-income consumers that have been stretched by cumulative inflation pressures,” Felhandler said. “They’re taking less trips to fast food.”

Analysts expect McDonald’s to bring in about $27.9 billion in revenue this year, up about 4%, and net income of about $9.1 billion, up about 6%. For 2027, they expect revenue of about $28.1 billion and net income of about $9.6 billion. In the third quarter, revenue rose 1% from a year earlier to $7.16 billion, while net income climbed 9% to $2.49 billion. Part of the reason why the income was climbing was selling company-owned restaurants to franchisees.

Through Nov. 20, McDonald’s stock was down about 11% this year, compared with a 0.9% rise in the S&P 500. But in the week ended Nov. 20, as an AI-led selloff pushed the S&P 500 down 8.6%, McDonald’s shares rose about 0.5%. They are up about 18% from their Oct. 7 low.
Yi bought McDonald’s shares at $233.59 on Oct. 2 to hedge her investment in Intel. To her, McDonald’s was an “old-timer stock” that can’t go wrong.
She sold on Nov. 6 at $278.79, about 19% higher. Yi said she doesn’t follow the company news at all. The stock had risen a lot, so she went with her gut and sold.
McDonald’s did not respond to a request for comment.
